part4_routeTypeDistribution.source: var/growth/google-war/latest.md 'By route type' section, computed from the now-populated indexation state (1225/1736 rows real, up from 31/1736)
part4_routeTypeDistribution.observation: Comparison inventory (1348 URLs) dominates the DISCOVERED_NOT_INDEXED population by sheer count (627 of the 777 sitewide) -- consistent with comparisons being the largest single inventory class by a wide margin.

part11_37_38_inventorySaturation.criticalFinding: 100% of software DISCOVERED_NOT_INDEXED pages (136/136) and 100% of comparison DISCOVERED_NOT_INDEXED pages (627/627) have ZERO observed GSC impressions. By contrast, only 4.8% of CRAWLED_NOT_INDEXED software pages (1/21) and 70.5% of CRAWLED_NOT_INDEXED comparison pages (275/390) show zero impressions.
part11_37_38_inventorySaturation.interpretation: Google is not crawling the DISCOVERED_NOT_INDEXED population because, as far as this site's own GSC data shows, there is no external search demand for almost any of it. This is NOT evidence of a technical, architectural, or crawl-budget defect -- it is consistent with Google's crawler behaving rationally given the demand signal it has. This directly falsifies the implicit premise behind selecting a 'high-value DISCOVERED_NOT_INDEXED treatment cohort' (Part 15): there is no real-demand subset of the DISCOVERED population to select from.
part11_37_38_inventorySaturation.totalInventoryContext: 80.3% of the entire comparison inventory (1082 of 1348 URLs) shows zero observed impressions, regardless of known indexation state -- a very large zero-demand long tail that predates and is broader than just the DISCOVERED_NOT_INDEXED bucket.
part11_37_38_inventorySaturation.part37_redTeamAnswer: Part 37 asks: 'Would a human reasonably want every one of these ~1,923 URLs in Google?' For the 627 zero-demand DISCOVERED comparison pages specifically, the honest, evidence-backed answer is: probably not most of them. These read as combinatorial pairings (every published comparison pair) rather than pages responding to an observed real buyer question. This is not a recommendation to delete or noindex them -- zero observed impressions is not proof of zero possible future value, and deletion/consolidation decisions require the stronger evidence bar Part 12 sets -- but it is a real, honest answer to the red-team question, not a defense of the inventory.

part5_urlAge.method: Compared each software page's data/software/{slug}.json 'accessed_at' field (last data-research date, a proxy for recency -- not necessarily exact first-publish date) across the three real indexation-state groups.
part5_urlAge.finding: DISCOVERED_NOT_INDEXED software pages are substantially newer on median (over a month later) than both INDEXED and CRAWLED_NOT_INDEXED pages. Combined with the zero-demand finding above, age is a real, honest, partial explanation for the DISCOVERED_NOT_INDEXED population: newer AND undemanded pages simply haven't earned a crawl yet, which is a fundamentally different situation from a page Google has actively examined and rejected (CRAWLED_NOT_INDEXED). Per Part 5's own instruction, this is recorded as a real confound, not invented as a crawl-quality problem.
part5_urlAge.caveat: accessed_at reflects when a product's data was last researched, not a verified first-publish date for the page itself -- a reasonable but imperfect age proxy.

part6_sitemapAnalysis.sitemapCoverage: 984/1782 (55.2%) of all crawlable public pages are actually listed in the sitemap.
part6_sitemapAnalysis.finding: 95% of confirmed-indexed pages (21/22) are sitemap-listed -- sitemap membership correlates strongly with eventually getting indexed. But sitemap listing does NOT reliably produce a crawl: 569 of the 984 sitemap-listed URLs with known state (58%) are still DISCOVERED_NOT_INDEXED or CRAWLED_NOT_INDEXED. This supports Part 6's concern that a large volume of low-priority inventory is being submitted with the same freshness/priority signal as high-value pages, diluting the sitemap's usefulness as a prioritization surface -- without proving it, since demand (not sitemap presence) looks like the dominant factor per the inventory-saturation finding above.
part6_sitemapAnalysis.noActionTaken: Per Part 36's own caution ('do NOT mass-remove URLs immediately... only execute if evidence strongly supports it and rollback is easy'), this session did not modify the sitemap. A controlled sitemap-priority experiment is real, evidence-motivated backlog, not executed this session given the risk profile of touching a sitewide production surface without a longer observation window planned in advance.
